title: Why Iran Reopened Hormuz Then Closed It Again in 6 Hours?
fullText: At sunrise on April 17th, Iran's top diplomat did something the entire world had been waiting 46 days to hear. He stood in front of the cameras and declared the Straight of Hormuz completely open. 6 hours later, before the day was even over, Iran's parliament speaker walked the entire thing back. The straight was closed again. The agreement was scrapped. The Iranian Revolutionary Guard issued a statement saying control had returned to its previous state. And in the space of those six hours, between the announcement and the reversal, the price of oil crashed by 11%. The American stock market hit an all-time record high, and global shipping companies began making frantic phone calls trying to figure out whether they should send their tankers into the Persian Gulf or not. This was not a minor diplomatic stumble. This was the largest single-day move in oil prices since the war started, triggered by an Iranian announcement that lasted less time than a normal American workday. By the time the markets closed in New York, $6 trillion in global asset value had moved one direction and then started moving the other. And the country that caused all of it, the country that holds the key to the world's most important shipping lane, had just shown the entire world that it cannot make up its mind from one breakfast to the next lunch. By the end of this video, you will fully understand exactly what happened in those 6 hours. Why Iran's own government contradicted itself in public. what the Iranian Revolutionary Guard did behind the scenes to force the reversal and why the chaos inside Tyrron tells you more about the actual state of the regime than any military analysis you have read in the last 6 weeks. Let us start with what actually happened in plain sequence because the timeline is the entire story. On the morning of April 17th, Iran's foreign minister Abbas Aragchi gave an official statement. The straight of Hormuz, he said, was completely open for the duration of the ceasefire in Lebanon. Commercial shipping could pass freely. The Iranian government would not interfere with traffic. This was the first time since February that any senior Iranian official had publicly committed to keeping the straight open. The announcement was treated as a diplomatic breakthrough. Oil traders around the world saw it on their screens within minutes. The news services pushed it out as breaking. By 11 in the morning Eastern time in the United States, the price of American crude oil had dropped from $14 per barrel to about $83 per barrel. That is an 11% crash in less than 3 hours. The Dow Jones Industrial Average jumped a,000 points. The SNP 500 hit an all-time record high. Every investor on Earth concluded that the Iran war was effectively over. Now, here is where it gets really interesting. By early afternoon, before the American stock markets had even closed, a different Iranian official took to the microphones. His name is Muhammad Ber Galibah. He is the speaker of Iran's parliament. He is also one of the most senior figures in Iran's hardline political establishment, and his statement was the exact opposite of his foreign ministers. Iran, he said, was scrapping the agreement to reopen the strait. So long as the American naval blockade of Iranian ports continued, the Strait of Hormuz would remain closed. The agreement was off the table. Effectively, the foreign minister's statement from a few hours earlier was being cancelled by the speaker of parliament in real time in front of the entire world. But here is the problem. The contradiction was not just between two Iranian officials. The Iranian Revolutionary Guard immediately published its own statement reinforcing Galibah's position. Control of the straight. the revolutionary guard said had returned to its previous state. In other words, the strait was closed again. Within 6 hours of the original opening, the Iranian government had publicly disagreed with itself. And the part of the government that actually controls the navy and the missiles had sided with the people saying close it. You need to understand why this matters before we go any further. In a normal country, the foreign minister and the parliament speaker do not contradict each other in public on the most important international decision of the year. In a normal country, before a senior official announces a major policy reversal on global television, somebody in the chain of command checks with the people who actually have to enforce that policy. The fact that Aragchi made the announcement and Galibbah canceled it within hours tells you something specific. There is no functioning chain of command inside Iran right now. Different parts of the Iranian government are operating independently. The diplomatic side is trying to make a deal. The military side is refusing to allow it and nobody anywhere has the authority to settle the disagreement. Think about what that looks like from the outside. An oil tanker captain sitting in his ship somewhere in the Indian Ocean getting ready to enter the Persian Gulf is now being told two completely different things by the Iranian government within the same news cycle. Is the straight open? Yes, it is open. No, it is closed again. Yes, you can pass. No, you cannot pass. The captain has no idea whether his crew is going to be safe, whether his cargo is going to make it, or whether his ship is going to be sailing into a minefield. 600 ships are sitting outside the straight waiting for a clear answer. They got two answers in six hours. They are still waiting. Now, stop and think about what this 6-hour collapse actually tells you about the state of the Iranian regime. For decades, Iran has projected an image of unified hardline resistance. The Supreme Leader spoke and everybody fell in line. The Revolutionary Guard executed orders. The diplomats said what they were told to say. That is the picture the regime has carefully cultivated since the 1979 revolution. What you saw on April 17th was the public collapse of that image. The diplomat said one thing, the parliament said another, and the revolutionary guard sided with the parliament against the government's own foreign ministry. Is this the moment when the world finally realized that the Iranian regime is no longer one government, but several factions fighting each other in real time? or is it Iran's last successful trick where the chaos itself is part of the negotiating strategy designed to keep the United States off balance? One side says the regime is breaking apart in front of our eyes. The other side says this is sophisticated psychological warfare from a regime that has survived for 45 years by being unpredictable. Write your answer in the comments because the people who say Iran is collapsing and the people who say Iran is playing chess are about to have a very heated argument under this video. And it gets worse for Iran. The economic reality behind these six hours is the part most American news outlets are not connecting clearly. Iran cannot actually afford to keep the straight closed much longer. The numbers are public. They have been confirmed by multiple analysts and they are brutal. Iran is losing roughly $435 million per day in oil revenue because of the United States blockade. That is over$1 13 billion dollars per month. Iran's onshore oil storage capacity, the tanks where crude oil sits before it gets loaded onto export tankers, is approximately 50 to 55 million barrels. 60% of that capacity is already full. According to multiple American analysts, Iran has roughly 13 to 16 days of storage capacity remaining. After that, the oil has nowhere to go. Iran will be forced to shut down its oil fields, which damages them physically and takes weeks or months to restart. Once the fields shut down, Iran's only source of foreign currency stops generating money, and the regime starts running out of cash to pay its soldiers. That is the deadline that drove Iraqi to make his announcement on the morning of April 17th. Iran's diplomatic side understands the math. They know the strait has to reopen or the Iranian economy collapses inside of two weeks. They tried to make the announcement that would save them. And the Revolutionary Guard, the part of the government that benefits from chaos and instability, shut it down within hours. Because for the Revolutionary Guard, an Iran that is desperate and isolated is an Iran where they have power. An Iran that makes a deal with the United States is an Iran where they lose relevance. There is another angle that almost nobody is talking about. While the foreign minister and the parliament speaker were contradicting each other in public, Pakistan's army chief, a man named Aim Munir was sitting in Thrron trying to mediate between the United States and Iran. Pakistan of all places has emerged as the country trying to broker an end to this war. Munir flew into Thran on April 15th carrying a new message from Washington. He met with Iran's foreign minister, with the parliament speaker, and reportedly with senior revolutionary guard officials. He spent two days trying to coordinate a path forward. And while he was sitting in Iranian government offices trying to put a deal together, the Iranians were publicly contradicting themselves on the most important issue of the war. That is the diplomatic environment Pakistan is trying to navigate. Now, here is where this starts affecting people who do not follow geopolitics. Every American family paying for gas at the pump, just watched their fuel costs swing wildly inside of one news cycle. Brent crude oil, the global benchmark, dropped from $13 per barrel to $90 per barrel and then started climbing back up. American gasoline prices, which had been hovering at $4.13 per gallon, briefly looked like they might come down to manageable levels for the first time since the war started. American stock investors saw their retirement accounts gain real value as the markets rallied to record highs. And then 6 hours later, the entire move started reversing as the news of Iran's reversal spread through the trading floors. The volatility itself was the cost. Oil traders who price risk into every barrel started building permanent risk premiums into the global oil price because they no longer trust any Iranian announcement. That risk premium gets paid [music] by every American at every gas station, every grocery store, every truck delivering goods. The Israel side of the story matters, too, because Iran's original announcement was specifically tied to it. Arachi did not just open the straight. He opened the straight for the duration of the ceasefire in Lebanon. The same morning on April 17th, President Trump announced a 10-day ceasefire between Israel and Lebanon, brokered by his administration, Iran took that ceasefire as the opening they needed to make their own move. They linked the strait to Lebanon. As long as Israel stopped attacking Hezbollah in Lebanon, Iran would let the strait stay open. That was the deal Aragchi offered. Within hours, two things happened that killed it. First, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu publicly said Israel was not actually leaving Lebanon. The Israeli military, he said, would remain in a 10 km security buffer zone in southern Lebanon indefinitely until Hezbollah was disarmed. That is not a ceasefire in any meaningful sense. That is a continuation of the Israeli operation under a different name. Second, the Revolutionary Guard inside Iran refused to accept any deal that left an American blockade in place. Both ends of the deal collapsed at the same time, and the straight reversal followed within hours. This is where the conversation fundamentally changes. The April 22nd ceasefire deadline is now exactly 4 days away. The original 2e ceasefire that started on April 8th expires next Wednesday. If there is no agreement by that date, both sides are technically free to resume hostilities. Iran's economy will be one or two weeks from forced shutdown of its oil fields. The American blockade will have been in continuous operation for over 10 days. The Israel Lebanon situation will still be unresolved and the Iranian government will still be unable to issue a single coherent statement about its own strategic position as the events of April 17th proved on live television. Stop and think about what the Iranian regime actually looks like right now from inside. The Supreme Leader Mojaba Kame has not been seen in public for 49 days since being wounded on the first day of the war. His face is reportedly disfigured. He has lost the use of one or both legs and he communicates only through audio conferences. The foreign minister who tried to make the deal on April 17th has been publicly humiliated by his own parliament. The parliament speaker who scrapped the deal does not actually control the revolutionary guard and the revolutionary guard itself which controls the navy and the missiles has effectively become the dominant decision-making body inside Iran. There is no single voice in Thran. There is no functioning chain of command. Think about what that means for the people in Washington trying to negotiate this thing to a conclusion. Vice President J. D. Vance flew to Islamabad on April 11th to meet with Iranian negotiators for 21 hours of marathon talks. Those talks failed because the Iranian negotiators in the room could not actually commit to anything. Every concession had to be sent back to Thrron for approval. The Americans were negotiating with people who did not have the authority to close the deal. That is exactly what happened again on April 17th. The foreign minister announced a deal. The parliament canceled it. The revolutionary guard reinforced the cancellation. The same dynamic that broke the Islamabad talks has now broken the announcement that was supposed to end the war. Is the Iranian regime actually in the process of falling apart with the chaos visible to anyone watching? Or is the United States now in the position of trying to negotiate with a country that does not have a real government, where every deal gets undone within hours by whichever faction did not like it? One side says this is what regime collapse looks like in slow motion and the United States should keep the pressure on until the chaos becomes impossible to manage. The other side says this is what makes the situation extremely dangerous because a country with no clear command structure can stumble into a catastrophic decision in any direction. Write where you stand in the comments because the people who say America should press harder and the people who say this is the moment to ease off are going to have a serious argument under this video. And there is one more piece that ties the whole picture together. The Revolutionary Guard, the part of the Iranian government that killed the deal on April 17th, has every reason to want this war to continue. For the Revolutionary Guard, the war is the source of their power. As long as Iran is at war, the guard runs the country. The civilian government, the foreign ministry, the elected parliament, all of them become subordinate to the security apparatus. When there is an external threat, the moment the war ends, the moment a real deal is signed with Washington, the Revolutionary Guard has to give up some of its control. The military commanders go back to being just military commanders. The diplomats start running policy again. The Guard's grip on Iran's economy, on the smuggling networks, on the foreign currency flows, all of it weakens. So when the foreign minister tried to open the door to a deal on the morning of April 17th, the Guard had a clear institutional reason to slam that door shut by the afternoon. They were not protecting Iran. They were protecting their own position inside the Iranian system. So here is the question that matters. The most important diplomatic announcement of the entire war lasted 6 hours before being cancelled by Iran's own government. The American blockade is in its sixth day and has reduced Iranian oil exports to almost zero. Pakistan is shuttling between Thran and Washington trying to put together a deal that the Iranian government cannot actually agree to internally. The ceasefire expires in 4 days and the Iranian Revolutionary Guard has now publicly proven that it has the power to overrule its own foreign ministry on global television. Is this the inflection point where the Iranian regime collapses from within with the United States simply waiting for the inevitable? Or is this the moment where Iran becomes the most dangerous regime on Earth? Because nobody anywhere knows who is actually making decisions for the country with 2,000 ballistic missiles, hundreds of fast attack boats, and a straight that 20% of the world's oil has to pass through. One side says the regime is finished and Trump has already won. The other side says a regime with no chain of command is the most dangerous regime in the world right now.
